newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Man dug grave for family killed by Serbs.
newsitem.headline: Man dug grave for family killed by Serbs.

text.p: An elderly Bosnian Moslem man has led investigators to a grave that he said he secretly dug for his wife, daughter and granddaughter after they were shot in a wartime massacre on Serb-held territory.
The tomb, thought to contain civilians executed by separatist Serbs near Gorazde in 1992, was one of a series exhumed by government teams since the 1995 Dayton peace treaty.

But the origin of this one had unusual emotional poignancy because, according to the man, he crossed front lines during the war -- risking his life -- to find the bodies strewn in a wood and buried them as a minimally dignified farewell.

Leaning on a cane, 65-year-old Hasib Muslic led investigators on Sunday to a wooded ravine 20 km (12 miles) southeast of Gorazde, territory returned by the Serbs to the Bosnian government under the Dayton accords.

There the team exhumed a shallow grave containing Muslic's wife, daughter and granddaughter. He said they were part of a group of Moslem women and children villagers caught hiding in the forest by Serb paramilitaries on May 9, 1992.
The Serbs had been marching menfolk away from the hamlet of Vuciji Potok when they spotted the women and children. "A girl survived and gave the story," said Muslic.

"They were detected by one Serb who fetched a fellow soldier, who arrived and shot nine women and children at once, including my 50-year-old wife, daughter and her 16-month-old daughter," he told Reuters Television.
Investigators said 28 other grave sites containing executed women and children were believed scattered along the ravine.
"The Serbs didn't dig any grave for the nine, they just left the bodies crumpled there," said Muslic.
"So I secretly returned on June 13, 1992, sneaking across front lines. I found my family and buried them along with another woman's body that was there."
The investigators unearthed a grave nearby containing what they said were the bodies of sisters aged six and nine years old. The skull of one had a bullet hole.
Moslems who have resettled in the area said they were all burned out of their homes by Serb paramilitaries in May 1992.

The International Criminal Tribunal on former Yugoslavia, based in The Hague, has indicted 75 people for atrocities against civilians and prisoners in Bosnia and Croatia in 1991- 95. The majority of indictees are Serbs.
Tribunal investigators recently excavated several mass graves of Moslems slaughtered by the Serb conquerors of the eastern town of Srebrenica in mid-1995.
